speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to comment today on the Minister of Finance's Budget Speech.
The Budget Speech describes services the Government of Canada wants to make available to Canadians, as well as the revenues necessary to pay for their distribution. For years, the Government has made services available to Canadians but Trudeau, who called himself a Liberal although, deep down inside, he was an idealist and a socialist, did it for 20 years with the co-operation of both Opposition parties- For 20 years, we gave to Canadians, we offered them services and at every election we increased the promises for the services to be provided in future, but by borrowing from people who, when the promises were made, did not pay, were not even born or in some cases from teen-agers who today, tomorrow, and 30 years from now will still have to pay for the debts of the Liberals, supported by the socialists.
Those debts, Mr. Speaker, amount to $320 billion. That was the key point in drawing up our budget speech. How can you live with a $320-billion debt? How can you live with interest costing Canadians $3 million an hour or $80 million a day? How can you live with interest costing every Canadian $1,300 a year or a family $5,000 a year? That is the cost for every family in Canada-$5,000. It costs every Canadian family $400 a month to pay the interest on the services provided by the Liberal Government, in alliance with the socialists, over the last 20 years, just to get elected every four years!
May 8, 1989

That is the reality we Conservatives must continue to face today.
What are the effects of this debt today, Mr. Speaker? It means that the Government, with such a great need for money, must borrow more. And when demand for money is strong, bankers must raise interest rates. Government competes with private enterprise, both multinationals and small businesses, and then companies must pay more for the money they need to grow. And in turn, Canadians who must buy an automobile, furniture, sporting goods, or have to build additions to their homes, must pay higher interest costs because the Canadian Government needs money to service an extremely heavy debt. This impacts negatively on small and medium businesses, borrowers, consumers. In that light we had to exercize caution and make the best out of this financial situation. We could have raised taxes, thereby choking demand in Canada. This would have met the current inflationary trends head on, but there was a danger. If through our actions we dampened demands too much, another problem would arise, and we would be faced with another recessionary bout. So what does it take?
It takes the most balanced Budget possible, one that will not fuel into the existing inflation, and it also takes a Budget that will not lead us into a serious recession. To reach that goal we decided, first, to increase the federal Government's revenues by having the workforce pay part of our obligations, rather than, as has been done over these last 20 years by a Liberal administration, having our commitments and our present needs shouldered by our young people still in university, high school and elementary schools. We do not want to have them pay for our debts later on.
We want to leave them a nice legacy. We do not want to leave them debts built up by the Liberals. So we decided, first, to reduce Government expenditures by $1.5 billion and increase Government revenues by $3.5 billion.
Some will say we could have reduced Government expenditures further. True! But we would have hurt a lot of people-it would have hurt our seniors, chronic patients, young people in school, it would have hurt a part of the people who need to share in our common wealth. So we reduced our expenditures by $1.5 billion, a maximum in our view. We discontinued some services we felt were neither essential nor a priority. People sug-
The Budget-Mr. Fontaine
gested we could have made further cuts. We could have indeed.
But, Mr. Speaker, keep in mind that services may be curtailed, and some Canadians who work for Crown corporations or for the Government have just been told they will be laid off. Of course they will find employment elsewhere, but by the time they do find new jobs the Government will spend a lot more than their annual salary because there are expenses to be paid in cases of severance. If an employee who has been working for the Government or a Crown corporation for 10, 15 or 25 years and earning $30,000 or $35,000 a year is told he will be out of work tomorrow, employment termination may cost twice as much in some cases. So when we reduce operating expenses by $35,000, in some cases we increase costs to reduce this expense on the long term, but for the coming year expenses will go up, sometimes by $70,000. This is why we were unable to reduce our expenses by more than $1.5 billion.
By contrast, Mr. Speaker, a trend is unmistakable in the ever sharper decline in our expenses since 1984. Canada's Gross National Product that year stood at about $500 billion and at the time-the Liberals had been in office for 20 years-the Government did absorb, manage and look after one fifth of that amount. By 1994 we expect that public outlays or the Government's share of the GNP should be down to about 15 per cent, and this would then work out to 15 per cent of roughly 1,000 billion dollars.
Since the Budget Speech was made on April 27, Mr. Speaker, I have spent the weekends in my riding meeting true Canadians, real ordinary Canadians who are responsible for the collective wealth of our country, who do not live as parasites, but who have jobs, operate small businesses, or carry out their respective duties as educators, teachers, physicians, or nurses. When I met them, they asked me a few questions about our Budget. Some wanted to know if in our Budget we had cut the resources made available to the Canadian International Development Agency. I replied that we had in fact reduced our contribution by $360 million because we felt that according to an old saying which is worth repeating here, charity begins at home. It is an old saying which is still true today. We can also assure the people in Third World countries who are still getting more than $2.4 billion from the Canadian Government that we are in the process of strengthening our own economy in Canada and that as soon as we have achieved this goal, we will have even more resources available to help countries in

May 8, 1989
The Budget-Mr. Fontaine
need. But before we can share our resources, Mr. Speaker, we must first and foremost be able to collectively control our own economy.
Other people asked why we had reduced Old Age Security pensions? I replied to them that we had absolutely not reduced Old Age Security pensions. I explained that Canadians who have net incomes of $50,000 today and who are eligible for Old Age Security pensions have nothing whatsoever to do with those other Canadians who are getting both the Old Age Security pensions and the Guaranteed Income Supplements. This measure applies only to 4 per cent of Canadians 65 years of age or over and who are earning in excess of $50,000. For instance, a Canadian earning $52,000 will have to pay 15 per cent on the excess $2,000, that is, $300. This Canadian will therefore see his Old Age Security pension reduced by $300. In addition to that, the Old Age Security pension will disappear alltogether for 2 per cent of Canadians who are 65 years of age or over. That will increase Government revenues or reduce expenditures by $600 million.
Others have asked us why we did not plan to continue Government intervention in unemployment insurance. Why, Mr. Speaker, would the Government help me insure my house or my car? Is it the Government's responsibility to pay insurance premiums on my car?
The same applies to people who work. Workers can get insurance from the Unemployment Insurance Commission, which was put in place by the Government. They insure themselves against losing their jobs. We reduced payments slightly but we told those people: "OK, you will get a little less each week, but we will help you find another job faster. We are going to train you so that you can find another job fast.'' That is one thing we are offering workers.
Also, when we came to power in 1984, the unemployment rate was 11.6 per cent; today it is 7.8 per cent. We created 1,5 million jobs for Canadians.
We will reduce unemployment and make the fund self-supporting. We will give money to unemployed Canadians to make their training easier and we intend to curb unemployment insurance abuse. Everybody knows that people throughout the country systematically abuse this generous system at the expense of all Canadians. This must stop, Mr. Speaker, and we have taken action to stop it.
People have asked me why the increase for individual income tax, after we had reduced it. The answer, Mr. Speaker, is that in 1989-90, the tax increase for those earning $30,000 will be $80 a year. That is not even $2 a week. The tax increase for those earning $60,000 will be $240 a year, $20 a month or $5 a week as their share in restoring our country's finances. Is that asking Canadians too much in a difficult period? And for Canadians who earn $100,000, it will be $725 a year.
Mr. Speaker, those are the questions I was asked. In general, people are pleased with our budget, especially seniors, because they know from experience in life that nothing can be given that has not already been earned. Seniors do not want us leaving our debts to their grandchildren. So they are pleased that finally a government can continue to shoulder its responsibilities and put our country on the right track.
And finally, Mr. Speaker, we also said in our budget speech that we intended to modify our tax system by bringing in a new tax on goods and services to replace the tax on manufactured products. The main reason for this change is that the tax on manufactured products is unfair. For example, Mr. Speaker, take the company that makes this chair here.
So it is Canadian or American. If the chair sells for $400 the Canadian maker today would add a $48 tax to the cost of the chair and he will bid to sell it in the United States or anywhere in Canada. The American makes the same chair, he bids anywhere in Canada or the United States, but he does not have to contend with the 12 per cent tax on manufactured goods. So he can offer to sell his chair for $400 whereas the Canadian must market it at $448. This is why the tax on manufactured goods throws fair competition out of kilter. We had to eliminate the problem, and that is precisely what we will achieve with our goods and services tax. The goods and services tax will enable Les poulies Maska, a company located at Sainte-Claire very close to the riding of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Blais) to sell Cadillac brakes to General Motors in the United States without this 12 per cent tax which is shutting the company off its markets.
This will also enable Ressorts Cascade in the riding of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development to continue selling springs in the United States, whereas the 12 per cent levy was getting to be an export barrier. And the same thing goes for Salaisons Brochu in my riding. The company will go on selling ham in the United States without this tax at every stage of produc-
May 8, 1989

tion. That is why we did away with that tax. It will generate revenues to replace the tax on manufactured goods-$16 billion-and the Government will secure additional revenues and give credits to less fortunate people so they will not suffer from the goods and services tax.
Nor will this tax apply to such basic commodities as food, prescription drugs and medical devices. The tax will not apply if you sell the existing house in which you live. It will apply to new homes sold by builders, but perhaps it will come cheaper because up till now the 12 percent tax sometimes hits twice the same home built by a contractor. So to people who have to sell their homes, two, three, four, five or ten years down the road I say not to worry, the tax will not apply; it applies on new homes as sold by builders. It does not apply to housing, it does not apply to university education. Low-income people will receive four times a year a credit they can apply towards that tax.
So this was the essence of our tax message for our second term. We moved by steps to free ourselves from the hazardous economic situation put in place by the Liberals and the Socialists, as Hon. Members are aware. By steps we want to break free and better control our lives. The most important message, Mr. Speaker, is to tell our children: We will not leave you in debt. We are going to leave you an active Canada, with opportunities for a quality life. This was the essence of our message, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this tax message is four years late. In 1984 your own Leader and the present Minister of Linance stated that within four years they would bring the deficit down to $7 billion. This has not been done, even in four years. Is that your tax message? European economists will not invest in Canada for the simple reason the Canadian Government is increasing taxes instead of making cuts where needed. If less money was taken away from Canadians, they would be interested in investing here. Is that your tax message? In view of the fact that from 1984 to 1988 you had a $82 million surplus? It is like someone in debt who for the next four years has significant surplus income. When this happens, we arrange to pay our debts. But, you increased it instead, and now you come here and give us a tax message?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to have heard the Hon. Member for Gatineau-La Lievre (Mr. Assad) in 1984. When we came to power, we had an annual
The Budget-Mr. Fontaine
Budget of $38 billion, but we managed to bring that down. And when we did, your colleagues who were there at the time screamed bloody murder because we managed to reduce the Budget! You should have been there. You should have heard them. You should have read what they said. They objected to our tax increases that were aimed at reducing the deficit, and they also objected to our spending cutbacks. You should have been there!
These people also said that because of the Budget proposals made in 1984 and the years after that, unemployment would rise. The Budget did not cause unemployment. Thanks to the budgets we brought down in 1984 and in subsequent years, we were able to help the private sector create 1.5 million new jobs during the past four years.
When you mentioned European investors who were avoiding Canadian markets, you were wrong, because today, Europeans consider Canada as the promised land for setting up business and developing their American markets, all because of the Free Trade Agreement both your colleagues and the non-elected senators objected to. European investment is rising. You should do your homework. When we speak in the House, we try to inform Canadians, not play politics and mislead them.
You mentioned the debt has increased. Would you like to know why? It has increased because we have to pay the interest that is accumulating on the enormous debt you passed on to us in 1984. And if you take the debt increase, plus $30 billion in interest per year, it adds up to the difference between what we had when we came to power and what we have today. We managed to keep the debt down to that level and we also managed to improve the state of the economy and increase employment in Canada. You never did that during the 20 years you were in power!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a couple of questions for the Hon. Member. He said in his speech that seniors in his riding have a lifetime of experience and do not want to leave their grandchildren with a debt. Has he read the National Pensioners and Senior Citizens Federation submission to the Government of February, 1989 in which it shows that they passed a resolution unanimously urging the Government to eliminate payment of income tax from all Canadian families or individuals whose income is at or below the accepted poverty level? They go on to say that there are numbers of seniors in this country, particularly women, who are in fact living below the poverty line because their only source of income is

May 8, 1989
The Budget-Mr. Fontaine
the old age security and the guaranteed income supplement.
Does the Hon. Member not believe that those seniors, while they respect the need for fiscal responsibility, also understand very clearly how important it is to be able to eat well and be properly sheltered in their declining years? The Hon. Member refers to the new proposed sales tax and talks about the unfairness of it. I think we all accept that there are inequities in the current manufacturers' tax. But is it fair that the kids and moms in this country will be paying tax on clothes for children, on music lessons and on family counselling? Is that fair, Mr. Speaker?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the first thing I would like to say to the Hon. Member is that according to our previous economic message, as you well know, barely 10 per cent of Canadians 65 years old and over pay income tax. In fact, every day your Leader has been asking us to make them pay more taxes. These 10 per cent have worked in the course of their lives and accumulated a certain amount of wealth. They are paying income tax today, and your Leader wants us to change their tax rate and make them pay more. That is the answer to the first part of the question.
Second, you said that the elderly need a pension. We are aware of that. Senior citizens need a pension, but Canadians who are still in the labour force are entirely aware of the fact that we can go on giving them this pension and give our seniors the security they need, and that is very important. Senior citizens want to be sure they will receive their pension cheque every month. They know that Canadians who are in the labour force must have jobs to help pay for those cheques. And that is the kind of economic climate we have given them. We have created one million and a half new jobs since 1984. These people contribute to the public Treasury and ensure that senior citizens receive their pension cheques regularly.
About the goods and services tax, I said that it applied to all goods. I gave a list of exemptions, and I said that it replaces the old system and does not create new revenue. It does not penalize our young people because there are people living confortably who will still receive a cheque four times a year to compensate for the sales tax.
They will receive a cheque that says it is for the sales tax they have paid during the last three months. People who are just making ends meet and are living barely above the poverty level won't have to worry, because they will get a refund in advance.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Having heard what my friend the Hon. Member for Levis (Mr. Fontaine) had to say, Mr. Speaker, I find it very hard to keep cool because a great many things he said are not consistent with the facts.
He tries to portray this Government as a political Robin Hood, a Government that robs from the rich through this claw-back and gives to the poor.
First, the Hon. Member makes the mistake of treating family benefits and pensions as some kind of hand-out, which they are not. We in this Party see those services as being a social contract with Canadian citizens, giving meaning and purpose to what we call Canadian citizenship. Second, he did not talk about the thresholds going down next year. He did not talk about medicare being put in a similar situation one day.
More important and more misleading is the tax situation facing Canadians. Canadians want to know why the Government is imposing such an unfair tax burden which will apply differently depending on who one is, where one lives, and how much one makes. Canadians do not mind paying their way for future generations. They do not mind putting their shoulders to the wheel, digging down, contributing and pushing Canada forward. However, when Canada moves forward, Canadians do not want people to be left behind.
We must examine not only this Budget because we cannot look at it in isolation, but the previous four Budgets. There have been five Budgets handed down by this Government. We have been asking in the House of Commons since the most recent Budget was introduced what the cumulative impact of these Budgets is on an average family in my riding. My riding is a hard working, middle-class type of riding, and I would imagine it is very similar to that of the Hon. Member for Levis (Mr. Fontaine). People in my riding are saying that after four or five Budgets, it is becoming more difficult to stay in the working middle-class sector of Canadian society.
May 8, 1989

They fall off on either one side or the other. The disparity between the extremes is getting bigger.
Let us look at the numbers. After five Conservative Budgets, a person earning $100,000 pays 8 per cent more in taxes. The guys and gals earning $30,000 will have to pay 60 per cent more in taxes. I ask the Hon. Member to try to explain that to Canadians. He should try to sell it. Canadians know an unfair tax system and an unfair Budget. I would ask the Hon. Member to address that unbalanced, unfair and inequitable situation that the Government has created rather than masquerade as some political Robin Hood which the Government is not.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will try to summarize the issue. I am not sure whether he knows exactly what was his question. I think I heard him say that my Government was abandoning the poor, the sick and the aged. With the Socialists' assistance, the previous Liberal Government had systematically abandoned future generations of Canadians leaving them to pay the debts incurred by this generation and thus finding a way to stay in power longer. Mr. Speaker, these are the people who did abandon generations. We, on the contrary, are trying to assume our responsibilities. I must emphasize the fact that ever since we came to power, we have created jobs for over a million Canadians to help us develop this country. Far from abandoning them, we are taking them along. You had abandoned them! We have put an end to this practice. Now, all Canadians must strive to increase the collective wealth to ensure the availability of our social programs for the aged, the sick and the young.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 spent last weekend in the riding represented by the Hon. Member for Levis (Mr. Fontaine) to witness the launching of the new Joseph and Clara Smallwood ship.

During my brief visit to his riding, I got the impression that the Hon. Member was a reasonable fellow. I was a little taken aback today when I realized that he was defending this foul Budget without equivocation.
Is the Hon. Member not really bothered by the manifest duplicity of this Budget? Last fall the spokespersons for his Party were saying the exact opposite. They were saying that everything is coming up roses, that
The Budget-Mr. Rodriguez
there is no problem. They could not pronounce the word "deficit". They never mentioned it at any time.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of State (Agriculture)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: False.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He is awake. Welcome. We are here every day at this time. Come in more often.
I understand that we have hit a nerve. Last fall during the election campaign, there was not a word about the deficit. Everything was coming up roses. Things would be magnificent. We would all have two cars in every garage.
Now we are told what a terrible time it is and how terrible the Liberals were before 1984. Suppose we were to buy the thesis that everything was terrible before 1984, why has it taken almost five years for the people on that side of the House to discover that there is a problem? Last fall they did not know there was a problem. Is the Hon. Member not a bit bothered by this duplicity, this basic dishonesty that last fall we were told one thing and now we are being told something very different? They both cannot be right. They are mutually exclusive. Which is right, what we were told last fall or what we are being told now?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In 1984 and even in 1983 as we were striving to get rid of this Government, Mr. Speaker, we had exactly the same platform as today. We were as aware then as we are now that before giving money to the needy, we had to earn it. That is the difference between the Liberal Party which was led by a Socialist-a Socialist had become the Leader of the Liberal Party. First he got his membership card from the NDP, but he switched to the other side because he was a political opportunist.
These people were living off other people's money. The difference with us is that we know we must create wealth before sharing it. This is still our position. We have been on this track since 1984 and we shall keep on going down the path already staked out four years from now, and after we have again been re-elected, we will still continue in that direction, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am always delighted to follow the Hon. Member for Levis (Mr. Fontaine). Everyone has now heard from the extreme right, the voice of unreasonableness. Now we get to hear the voice of reason, of moderation and of concern.

May 8, 1989
The Budget-Mr. Rodriguez
Mr. Speaker, I thought about a theme for my contribution to this debate, and I have taken the theme of a question: On which side is this Government? To whom is this Government, under the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), accountable? Let me just draw a picture. We all have this very vivid picture of Brian Mulroney as a boy growing up in Baie Comeau. We all remember him. He sang for his breakfast. He sang for the bosses of the Iron Ore Company of Canada from Chicago. He sang for them and he got $50 American. That was big money in those days. Not so long ago, four years ago, he sang for his political boss. He sang in Quebec City for Ronald Reagan, he sang When Irish Eyes Are Smiling.
He has been singing his whole life for somebody else, for the people who pull his chain, the same corporate big-wigs that during the last election put up $2 million plus to advertise to Canadians for the re-election of the Mulroney Government, the same gang. Mr. Speaker, there is a saying that he who pays the piper calls the tune. They have called the tune. They have paid the piper, and now what are they doing? They have grabbed the pipe, and they are not only paying, they are playing the tune. There he is coming out of his basket, serpentine, sinuous and seductive. He is coming out of his basket and he is dancing to the tune. Whose tune is he dancing to? It is the same boys to whom he went for a very private and very secretive dinner meeting in Toronto one week before the Budget came down. Yes, he went to a private meeting in Toronto, possibly in the back rooms of Winston's. Now, who was the host of that secret meeting?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: John Turner?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, not John-I do not say the J.C. word here. It was Tony Fell of Dominion Securities. He was the host. Who were among the guests? Hal Jackman from National Trust. How about this one-Alf Powis from Noranda? How about Bob Martin from Consumers Gas, and my friend Bill James from Falconbridge, and Doug Creighton from The Toronto Sun, The Toronto Star, et cetera, Bob Osborne from MacLean Hunter, and who of all people, Dave Culver flew all the way from Montreal, the same person who headed up that campaign to get the Tories re-elected. These are the real boys. So what were the boys saying? Mr. Speaker, there he was having a nice, quiet, cosy supper before the
Budget came down, presumably assuring them that there is nothing in that Budget that was really going to touch them, that everything was safe.
Did the Prime Minister meet with a single mother who is looking for child care for her children and cannot get it? Did he meet with a single mother? He did not fly to the Toronto to meet with the real people. Did he fly to meet with any family earning about $30,000 a year in Metro-Toronto, a family who is trying to keep a roof over their heads and food in their cupboards? Did he meet with anybody like that? You bet your bottom dollar, he did not. Did he meet with people from Summerside to explain how he was going to shaft them? Not on your bottom dollar he did not. Did he meet with the unemployed from Belle Island? No, Mr. Speaker, not at all. I ask, whose side is this Government on? I painted the picture of Brian the snake coming out of the basket, and people laughed. But it is as true as I am standing here that those who paid for the Government's re-election are now in fact calling the tune.
I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that I have an image of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). I do not know if many Members around here know it, but his favourite sport is squash. I have this image, and it keeps recurring again and again in my mind of the Finance Minister playing squash with John Crowe, the Governor of the Bank of Canada. I have this image of the ball being the unemployed in this country, the low-income Canadians, middle-income Canadians, Canadians who cannot afford homes. I think of the poor children of the world, and as the Finance Minister whacks the ball with a right forehand against the front wall, the ball ricochets off the back wall, John Crowe catches it with his high interest rates, and he whacks it up against the side wall, and the big, almighty, powerful but with a lot of integrity and courage and competence, he catches with his backhand and flips them so carelessly against the wall and smashes that ball, Mr. Speaker, pulverizes the ball, and they are playing with a blue ball, and he pulverizes the ball. That is the image that I have of these people who are responsible for fiscal and monetary policy in this country.
One has a Budget that in fact sticks it to them on a fiscal level, and the other one has the high interest rates and is sticking it to them on a monetary level. There they are like a squash ball pulverized between these two big, tough, powerful squash players.
May 8, 1989

Mr. Speaker, I ask myself, why did the Prime Minister not meet with these people? These are the real Canadians in my view. These are the people who really contribute to building this country. We know that they pay most of the taxes to support this country anyway with their revenues. So why? Because I honestly believe that Canadians are starting to see that this Government has decided who their friends are. Their friends are from the corporate boardrooms.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is not the mothers of Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Of course not the moms, of course not the unemployed. They don't even understand. We heard of the Prime Minister's wife going to open a food bank here in Ottawa. Imagine that. I can just imagine it. Their own lifestyle epitomizes the chasm which exists between the people in this country who are poor and who do not have homes and those who have it all so posh and so plentiful.
The Minister of Finance has been touted as a man of considerable courage. They said he has so much integrity, so much competence. This is why the Prime Minister could not bounce him. We are told that Bay Street was up in arms. They were phoning the Prime Minister's office. The telex machines and the fax machines were running overtime. All of Bay Street were baying "Keep Mike, Keep Mike" because we are told that Mike Wilson, the Finance Minister, has courage and integrity and competence and he also has friends. His friends are in high places. His friends reside in the boardrooms. Does it take a lot of courage, I ask you, to cut spending in the foreign aid budget, to cut food for the starving of this world? Does it take guts to do that? Does it take a lot of courage to eliminate child care spaces in this country when there is a great and expanding need for it? At the same time, their friends in high places owe $35 billion in deferred taxes. Does it take a lot of courage?
The President of Costa Rica was here not so long ago and was introduced in the House. The Prime Minister said to the President:
We know the impact of poverty and violence in Central America. For this reason, Canadian economic assistance has more than tripled in the past decade and will increase significantly during the next.
The Budget-Mr. Rodriguez
This is the same Prime Minister with a Budget that takes millions of dollars out of our foreign aid over the next five years. Does it take courage to do that?
During the last campaign we heard a lot from the Prime Minister about the promises that had been made. We all remember those promises such as the upgrader at Lloydminster, Hibernia, and the tar sands. When we stated that those were promises that were being made before the election, we were told that they were not promises but that they were spending commitments. Now we are told that they are no longer in effect. They are gone. Is that integrity?
The Finance Minister stated the reason that he had to bring in such a tough Budget was that there was this sudden jump in interest rates after the election and it forced the Government to abandon all those spending commitments-promises. That whole business of spending commitments-Budgets, how it can play with words.
It is like the Prime Minister getting what was supposed to be a loan from the PC Canada Fund for all his personal expenses and Gucci shoes. When we pointed out that it was a loan and that it should have been recorded, it then became an advance. It was a loan-advance. Here we have spending commitments-promises. The Prime Minister said that he had to abandon them because of the sudden rise in interest rates. Last November during the election the interest rates were already three points higher than what the last Budget had forecast.
Everything the Finance Minister had forecast was blown to smithereens. That is not the hallmark of a competent Minister of Finance, or one with integrity, but he has a lot of courage. One can have a lot of courage with a squash ball and a nice big racket, and old John Crow and those other birds over at the Bank of Canada helping. It is pretty easy to smash them around.
Is it competent to continue as the Government has, even after making people pay? This is short-term pain for long-term pain. Even after all these squeezings, the Government is still projecting a deficit of $30 billion, and a projected national debt in 1991 of some $400 billion. What type of competence is that? That is managing debt. During the campaign we heard that this was a Government that knew how to manage change. It could not even manage to deliver a Budget without leaking it.
What we are now hearing from the Minister of Finance is "sharing the burden". As the Government claws back $320 million from the bank presidents and all these big wigs the Government claims it is clawing back this old age pension. If a person is non-resident in this

May 8, 1989
The Budget-Mr Rodriguez
country, he does not get anything clawed back. Therefore, E. P. Taylor does not get his old age pension clawed back. K. C. Irving does not get his old age pension clawed back. He is in the Bahamas. All those well-heeled Tories live somewhere else most of the year.
The Minister of Finance sees himself as the Robin Hood from Rockcliffe. He is clawing back $320 million. If he really wanted to share the burden, and this is a real suggestion for the Tories, he could have created another tax margin of 34 per cent. The maximum tax margin used to be 17 per cent and that was squashed into 5 per cent or 3 per cent. The highest is now 29 per cent. There is a margin at 29 per cent and another one could be created at 34 per cent for the real biggies. The Government could have raised $2 billion, and we would not have to tinker around with the principle of universality. We would not have to run after will-o'-the-wisps like E. P. Taylor, K. C. Irving, and a whole bunch of others. A further $2 billion could be raised. This would hit at those in the $500,000 club. Who is in that club?
The $500,000 club was referred to earlier by one of our speakers. There is A. J. de Grandpre, Chairman of BCE Inc. This is the man who was set up to tell us how we can phase in the Free Trade Agreement by trampolining people all over the country. He is making $852,900. Vic Rice gets $1,034,000,499. This is the man who closed down Massey-Ferguson in Brantford. There were 4,000 jobs lost, but he looks after himself pretty well. Here is a Liberal who did not do too badly at all. There had to be a Liberal in this pile. He was also a candidate. Frank Stronach ran against old Sine Stevens. Sine was a candidate, and then he wasn't.
He was a candidate for a whole year and on the eve of the election the Prime Minister found his integrity and said: "No, you are not a candidate any more", and poor old Sine was out on the street. Sine was sunk. Sine was sitting with his wife playing Let's Make A Deal. Anyway, Frankie baby is making $1,354,000. There is this guy Culver. He was the one at this little private, secret meeting at Winston's. He headed up the campaign to get the Tories re-elected. He is the President of Alcan Aluminium. He is making $1,454,259. He is a fellow who calls himself my friend, and I accept that. There is also Bill James, Chairman and President of Falconbridge.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He is a friend of yours?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is right. He made a contribution to my campaign, and don't forget it. With friends like these! His salary jumped 20 per cent to $1,689,533. That is real money. That is not an accounting-what did he call the deferred taxes-procedure.
How does the Government say it is going to tackle getting some money? It is going to put in surtaxes on corporations. If a corporation does not pay any taxes, it does not pay any surtax. There are 89,000 wealthy corporations in this country that did not pay taxes last year. Therefore they will not pay any surtax. There are a couple of thousand very wealthy Canadians who did not pay anything and who will continue not to pay anything.
People with $100,000 in taxable income paid an average federal-provincial tax rate of 53.88 per cent in 1987. With tax reform it dropped to 46.4 per cent in 1988. This Budget will inch it back up to 48 per cent in 1990. This is still a full 5 per cent lower than in 1987, but people with incomes in the $27,000 range will end up paying 5 per cent more than when tax reform started. That is the logic of the Robin Hood of Rockcliffe.
I come back to the original question with which I began: On whose side is the Government? Who pulls the chain of the Government? The answer is very clear. Those who are wealthy, those who are economically powerful determine the decisions that are made by the Government. So it has been with Liberals, so it is with the Tories.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for his dynamic contribution to this debate. I also want to remind him, in case he has read the Budget papers, of some information concerning the last part of his speech, when he talked about the surtax schedule based, for example, on income. I just want to say that the increased surtax amounts to $45 a year for taxpayers earning $20,000; $725 a year for people earning $100,000; and $2,175 a year for those earning $200,000. If that is not a progressive increase, I don't know what is. I think the Budget aims at protecting low-income individuals, and it would be dishonest for the Hon. Member not to recognize that fact. We have significantly increased the tax credits, and have asked the well-to-do to help us fight our debt and our deficit problem. So, I don't know where the Hon. Member got his information, but from
May 8, 1989

the figures he used, it is clear that his information does not reflect the real situation.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, those of us who have been here a long time and have had opportunities to look at the statistics which come from the Department of Finance with respect to those who pay taxes in Canada were impressed by the information last year that there were several thousand Canadians, very well heeled, who did not pay a penny of income tax. Those are not my figures. I am reporting figures from Revenue Canada.
I do not see what the Government has done in the Budget that in any way catches those people who have paid no tax in the past. Certainly, there is no minimum tax on corporations. In fact, if they do not pay any tax, they cannot pay any surtax.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while listening to the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), I could not help but think of a study that came out yesterday in the Toronto Star. It analysed the federal Budget brought down a couple of weeks ago. It showed how families living in poverty in Canada have a net tax increase as a result of the Budget.
Let me give the example of a single parent family with two children and an income of $20,000. They have a tax increase as a result of the Budget. There is income tax, excise tax, surtaxes, an increase in the manufacturers' sales tax.
The Government is putting a tax on poverty, a tax on the poor. While the Government put a tax on poor families, did it close off the loopholes for the rich? There are a lot of loopholes for the rich.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for that excellent question. In fact, there is one loophole that really angers Canadians and cries out for correction. I agree with the person who said: "Eliminate the interest deductibility provision on non-productive takeovers in Canada to ensure that large pools of capital are not diverted to useless empire building". I agree with the person who said that, who happens to be the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in his book: "Where I stood, 1983".

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is past tense.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Here he is, the Prime Minister in 1989, and corporations still have the ability to borrow large amounts of money for corporate takeovers and mergers and the interest that is payable on the money they borrow to do that is still tax deductible.
The Budget-Mr. Rodriguez
The Prime Minister said where he stood. It seems to me he is still standing there in 1983 while we are in 1989.
If that loophole were plugged, I am sure it would account for several hundred million dollars.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, surely the Hon. Member will recognize that over the last few years we have made a considerable effort to remove the loopholes which existed under former regimes.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No you haven't.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have a very long list of efforts we have made and are making this year to improve the equity in our tax system.
As far as corporation tax is concerned, I hope he will realize that this year we will be getting $1 billion from the corporations. This is a new tax.
If the Hon. Member wants to listen, I can tell him the loopholes that were closed. I am sure he is aware of them. We have made a very good effort to make it equitable for all citizens and ensure that those who have a greater capacity to pay and contribute to the solution of the problem, which we have explained at length in the House, will make a greater contribution.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I recall the first Economic Statement of the Government in 1984 in which it created the $500,000 capital gains tax exemption. It put that in place against all the advice it was getting from all over the country. At the same time it made changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act which treated severance pay, pension income, holiday pay as earned income for UIC. That involved a few dollars while, at the same time, it put in place a generous handout to the wealthy of this country.
Second, I say to the Minister that there are 89,000 profitable corporations which do not pay any tax at all. I recall the debate on television between the Leaders in 1984 in which the Prime Minister promised that there would be a minimum tax on corporations. We still have not seen that tax. Yet there are 89,000 profitable corporations that do not pay any tax.
In fact, the contributions to Revenue Canada are dropping in terms of corporate contributions to the revenues of this country. They are paying about 12 per cent of the total revenues collected while individuals have been paying an increasing load of total revenues collected in this country. People look for fairness in the tax system. They do not see that tax fairness, but see themselves being constantly taxed.
We know that as a result of this Budget the average family will be taxed $710 this year and $1,000 next year. Surely the Minister should not sit there and believe that

May 8, 1989
Supply
he can do all of those things they did for the wealthy while just ignoring average, ordinary Canadians and letting them pay, pay and pay.

The House resumed from Friday, May 5, consideration of the motion of Mr. Dingwall:
That, in the opinion of this House, the claw-backs proposed by the Minister of Finance with regard to the Old Age Security pensions and Family Allowances (1) undermine all Canadian social programs; (2) make easier future incursions against Old Age Security pensions and Family Allowances as well as other social programs, including medicare; (3) will fall most severely on Canadians of moderate means while costing the wealthy little; and That this House, therefore, condemn the Government for this attempt to violate this sacred trust.
